Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

Long-term, high-precision observation of the small variations of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface and of their distribution with superconducting gravimeters can provide information on the internal structure of the Earth, such as mantle motion, mass distribution, solid-Earth tides, groundwater and mineral distribution, as well as external data such as ocean tides and climate change. Superconducting gravimeters have high sensitivity (up to $10^{-9}$ of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface) and strong stability, and are the gravity-observation instruments widely used in the Earth sciences today. With the increase in the number of superconducting gravimeters distributed around the world, the establishment of observation networks and data sharing, new opportunities are offered for the development of the Earth sciences, the precise testing of the law of universal gravitation, and so on. Answer the following questions on the gravity change caused by the distribution of groundwater, the principle of the superconducting gravimeter, and related matters.

1) Assume that the Earth can be regarded as a uniform sphere of radius 6370 km, with gravitational acceleration at its surface $g_0=9.80\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$ (neglect the rotation of the Earth). Now at a certain place underground there is a spherical underground lake of diameter 20 km filled with water, whose centre is 15 km below the ground surface. Find the small change $\Delta g$ of the gravitational acceleration at the ground surface directly above the underground lake. The gravitational constant is $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$, and the density of water is $\rho_{\text{water}}=1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$.

2) The core component of a superconducting gravimeter is a superconducting spherical shell made of the metal niobium (Nb) levitated in a magnetic field; for ease of calculation it is simplified here to a thin superconducting ring (see Fig. a). The levitating magnetic field is provided by a quasi-Helmholtz coil, which consists of an upper and a lower coaxial thin superconducting coil with $\alpha N$ and $N$ turns respectively ($\alpha<1$) connected in series; the radius of each of the two coils and the distance between their centres are all equal to $R$. Before the superconducting gravimeter is adjusted, the currents in the Helmholtz coil and in the thin superconducting ring are both zero; the thin superconducting ring lies in the plane of the lower coil ($z=0$) and is coaxial with the coils. After the adjustment starts, an external power supply slowly applies a current $i_0$ to the quasi-Helmholtz coil; during this process an induced current is produced in the thin superconducting ring. The magnitude of $i_0$ is adjusted so that the thin superconducting ring is levitated exactly in the plane of the upper coil ($z=R$), as shown in Fig. a. Since the resistances of the superconducting coils and of the thin superconducting ring are both zero (the temperature where they are located is 4.2 K), after the superconducting ring has been stably levitated, the power supply providing the current of the superconducting coils is removed, and the current $i_0$ in the superconducting coils and the magnetic field it produces can both remain stable for a long time. The mass of the thin superconducting ring is known to be $m$, its diameter $D$ ($D\ll 2R$), and its self-inductance $L$. Near the plane of the upper coil, the $z$-component and the radial component of the magnetic induction $B$ produced by the quasi-Helmholtz coil can be approximately expressed respectively as

$$\begin{cases} B_z=B_0\left[1-\beta(z-R)\right] \\[4pt] B_r=\dfrac{1}{2}\beta B_0 r \end{cases}$$

where $B_0$ is the magnetic induction at the centre of the upper coil, $\beta$ is the radial coefficient, and $r$ is the distance from the axis. Using the known parameters of the above coils and of the thin superconducting ring, and the externally applied current $i_0$ in the coils, find

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-1-3-fig1.png

Fig. a

i) the expressions for $B_0$ and $\beta$;

ii) the expression for the induced current $I_0$ of the thin superconducting ring at its equilibrium position ($z=R$);

iii) the expression for the gravitational acceleration $g_0$ at the place where the superconducting gravimeter is installed.

3) To measure small variations of the gravitational acceleration precisely, the superconducting gravimeter uses the AC bridge balancing method. To understand its principle and to make the calculation easier, regard the thin superconducting ring as a thin "plate" of area $A$, and at positions symmetric above and below the thin superconducting ring, i.e. at $R+d/2$ and $R-d/2$, fix two metal plates of the same shape, also of area $A$, forming the two capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ of the upper plate with the superconducting "plate" and of the lower plate with the superconducting "plate", as shown in Fig. b. Then $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected with two identical sets of inductances $L_0$ and capacitances $C_0$ to form a bridge, which is connected to an AC power supply (whose frequency is much higher than the rate at which the gravitational acceleration varies), as shown in Fig. c. Suppose that at a certain moment the gravitational acceleration at the place of the superconducting gravimeter is $g$, the thin superconducting ring (superconducting "plate") is at its equilibrium position $z=R$, and the AC bridge is balanced; at this time the same DC voltage $V_C$ is applied across $C_1$ and $C_2$. When the gravitational acceleration changes by $\Delta g$, the bridge becomes unbalanced; the DC voltage on $C_1$ is increased by $\Delta V$ and at the same time that on $C_2$ is decreased by $\Delta V$, and the bridge reaches balance again. Give the relation between $\Delta g$ and $\Delta V$ (neglect the edge effects of the capacitors).

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

A car obtains its power from the combustion of the air and petrol in the engine cylinders; the output power of the engine is proportional to the mass of air entering the cylinders. To increase the power, many cars are fitted with a turbocharger, which compresses the air before it enters the engine cylinders so as to increase the air density; to increase the air density further, an intercooler is also used, so that the air enters the cylinders after its temperature has been lowered. In a typical arrangement, the initial pressure of the air entering the turbocharger is one atmosphere, $p_0=1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, and its temperature is $T_0=15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; after passing through the turbocharger the air is adiabatically compressed to $p_1=1.45\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$; then, passing through the intercooler, the air is cooled at constant pressure to the initial temperature $T_0$ and fills the cylinder. Assume that air is an ideal gas; the cylinder volume is known to be $V_0=400\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the molar mass of air $M=29.0\ \mathrm{g\cdot mol^{-1}}$, the ratio of molar heat capacities $\gamma=7/5$, and the universal gas constant $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

1) Find the mass of the air in the cylinder in this case; compared with the case without turbocharging and cooling, by what factor is the output power of the engine increased?

2) If there is no intercooler and the air, after being compressed by the turbocharger only, is fed into the cylinder, what is the corresponding mass of air? Compared with the case without turbocharging, by what factor is the output power of the engine increased?

3) In the thermodynamic processes through the turbocharger and the intercooler, find the work done by the surroundings on the gas entering the cylinder, and the entropy change of the gas in the cylinder in each of the two processes above.

Problem 5

Part of the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to the American scientist Arthur Ashkin for his pioneering work on optical trapping (optical tweezers). Optical tweezers use a focused laser beam to trap tiny particles; Fig. a is a schematic diagram of an experimental optical-tweezers set-up. A He-Ne laser emits laser light of wavelength $\lambda=632.8\ \mathrm{nm}$, with beam diameter $D_1=1.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ and output power $P=30\ \mathrm{mW}$. To make the trapping more effective, a beam expander can be added after the output laser beam. After reflection by a mirror, the laser beam is incident on a focusing objective of focal length $f=4.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, which converges the beam into the distilled water in a sample cell; the liquid in the sample cell contains a certain number of small polystyrene spheres, which may be optically trapped when they pass through the focal spot of the laser. The diameter of the small spheres is known to be $D_{\mathrm{b}}=2.0\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ and their density $\rho_{\mathrm{b}}=1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$; the refractive index of the optical glass of the sample cell is $n_{\mathrm{g}}=1.46$; the refractive index of the distilled water in the cell is $n_{\mathrm{w}}=1.33$; the thickness of the glass at the bottom of the sample cell is $d=1.0\ \mathrm{mm}$; the distance from the outer surface of the bottom of the cell to the centre of the focusing objective is $a=2.0\ \mathrm{mm}$; the temperature during the experiment is $T=300\ \mathrm{K}$; the refractive index of air is $n_{\mathrm{a}}=1.0$; the gravitational acceleration is $g=9.80\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$; the Boltzmann constant is $k_{\mathrm{B}}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}}$.

Fig. a [聚苯乙烯小球 = polystyrene sphere; 样品池 = sample cell; 聚焦物镜 = focusing objective; 扩束镜 = beam expander; He-Ne 激光 = He-Ne laser; 反射镜 = mirror]

1) Find the diameter of the focal spot of the laser beam focused in air by the focusing objective when no beam expander is added;

2) to improve the trapping, the output laser beam is expanded; the beam expander used consists of a concave lens of focal length $f_1=-6.3\ \mathrm{mm}$ and a convex lens of focal length $f_2=25.2\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find the distance between the two lenses and the diameter $D_2$ of the expanded parallel laser beam;

3) the expanded laser beam is focused by the focusing objective shown in Fig. a into the distilled water in the sample cell; in the paraxial approximation, find the distance from the centre of the focal spot to the inner surface of the bottom of the sample cell, and the diameter of the focal spot;

4) Fig. b is a geometrical-optics model of the force on a small sphere immersed in distilled water in a light-intensity gradient (simplified as two light beams of different intensities). The incident rays $\mathrm{L_1}$ and $\mathrm{L_2}$ are along the x axis, with optical powers $p_1=1.0\ \mathrm{mW}$ and $p_2=2.0\ \mathrm{mW}$ respectively; the angles between the directions of the rays after refraction by the small sphere and the x axis are as shown in Fig. b. Neglecting absorption and reflection losses of the rays during propagation, find the forces on the small sphere in the x direction and in the y direction, and find the ratio of each of them to the weight of the small sphere;

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-1-5-fig2.png

Fig. b. Simplified model for the analysis of the force on a small sphere in a light-intensity gradient

5) find the root-mean-square speed of a small sphere in distilled water at room temperature (300 K);

6) optical tweezers can also be understood through an optical potential-well model: after a parallel laser beam is focused by a lens, the optical potential well in the radial direction $\hat{r}$ is distributed as

$$U(r)=\begin{cases} -U_0\left(1-\dfrac{r^2}{b^2}\right), & \text{for } r\le b \\[4pt] 0, & \text{for } r>b \end{cases}$$

where $U_0=0.078\ \mathrm{eV}$, $b$ is a constant, and $r$ is the distance from the axis of symmetry. Up to what speed can a small sphere be trapped by the optical potential well?

7) The speed distribution function of the polystyrene spheres is known to be expressible as

$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}v^2e^{-\frac{mv^2}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}}$$

where $m$ and $v$ are respectively the mass and the speed of a small sphere, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. Analyse and compare the probabilities that polystyrene spheres of masses $m$ and $2m$ respectively are trapped by the optical potential well.

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

Looking up at the starry sky can stimulate people's boundless imagination. With the progress of science and technology, people's understanding of the universe keeps deepening; the solution of the mystery of the missing neutrinos, the direct detection of gravitational waves and the recent photograph of a black hole have aroused wide public interest in exploring the universe. How did humankind, using limited equipment, observe and study the vast universe and its important constituents, the stars? Can members of the public with a basic knowledge of high-school physics understand quantitatively the internal and external properties of a star, such as its size, mass, age, lifetime, composition and energy-production mechanism? Taking as an example the star on which we depend for our existence, the Sun, and following the historical development, try to build a model of the Sun step by step from the simple to the complex. Since the interior of the Sun cannot be observed directly, the model built must be tested from many aspects, such as age, radius, surface temperature, energy output, neutrino flux, and so on, all of which must be mutually self-consistent within the same model.

The following are known: the radius of the Earth is 6370 km; the gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$; the Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\cdot m^{-2}\cdot K^{-4}}$; the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; the electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}=0.51\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the proton mass $m_{\mathrm{p}}=938.3\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the deuteron mass $m_{\mathrm{D}}=1875.6\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the $^{3}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus mass $m_{^3\mathrm{He}}=2808.4\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$; the $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus mass $m_{^4\mathrm{He}}=3727.5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c$; the speed of light in vacuum $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$.

1) The Zhoubi Suanjing ("The Arithmetical Classic of the Gnomon", originally titled Zhoubi), a book written more than two thousand years ago, describes a method for measuring the ratio of the diameter $D$ of the Sun to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$ (also called 1 astronomical unit): take a long bamboo pole and chisel out its nodes so that its inside is open throughout; the inner diameter of the bamboo pole is $d$. Point this bamboo pole at the Sun and change the length $L$ of the pole until the solar disc exactly fills the inner tube of the bamboo pole.

i) Give the relation between the angular diameter of the Sun ($\Phi=D/S_{\mathrm{SE}}$) and $d$ and $L$;

ii) to reduce the error, $L$ must be long enough; what other methods are there to reduce the error?

iii) It is measured that $d=1$ cun and $L=8$ chi (10 cun make one chi); estimate the value of $\Phi$.

2) At certain special times (for example on 6 June 2012) the Earth, Venus and the Sun lie almost on one straight line; observed from the Earth, Venus then looks like a small black dot set in the solar disc and moves slowly; this is called a transit of Venus, as shown in Fig. a. The British astronomer Halley proposed in 1716 that observations of the transit of Venus be made jointly all over the world in order to measure the angular diameter of the Sun and the Sun–Earth distance. The periods of revolution of the Earth and of Venus, which revolve around the Sun in the same sense, are known to be 365.256 days and 224.701 days respectively, and the inclination between their orbital planes is very small. Neglect the rotation of the Earth.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-1-6-fig1.jpg

Fig. a. Schematic diagram of the transit of Venus on 6 June 2012 [凌始外切 = first contact (start of transit, external tangency); 凌始内切 = second contact (start of transit, internal tangency); 凌甚 = greatest transit; 凌终内切 = third contact (end of transit, internal tangency); 凌终外切 = fourth contact (end of transit, external tangency)]

i) The orbits of the Earth and of Venus can both be regarded as circles; find the ratio $r_{\mathrm{VE}}$ of the Sun–Venus distance $S_{\mathrm{SV}}$ to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$;

ii) on 6 June 2012, the transit of Venus was observed at a certain place as shown in Fig. a; calculate the ratio of the chord length $D_{\mathrm{P}}$ swept across the solar disc during the transit of Venus to the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$. If the distance between this chord and the centre of the disc is $h_{\mathrm{P}}=5D/16$, what is the angular diameter $\Phi$ of the Sun?

iii) To measure the Sun–Earth distance, the transit of Venus must be observed from different places on the Earth's surface, as shown in Fig. b. Suppose that two observers P and P′ on the same meridian, whose straight-line distance (projected onto the direction perpendicular to the direction of observation) is $H$, observe the transit of Venus at the same time. For P, the path of Venus on the solar disc is AB and the observed transit time (the time interval during which the centre of Venus sweeps across the solar disc) is $t_{\mathrm{P}}$; for P′, the path of Venus on the solar disc is A′B′ and the observed transit time is $t_{\mathrm{P'}}$. Find the expression for the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$ (in terms of $\Phi$, $r_{\mathrm{VE}}$, $T_{\mathrm{E}}$, $T_{\mathrm{V}}$, $t_{\mathrm{P}}$, $t_{\mathrm{P'}}$, $H$, etc.).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-1-6-fig2.png

Fig. b. Schematic diagram of the transit of Venus [地球 = Earth; 金星 = Venus; 太阳 = Sun]

iv) The latitudes of Beijing and Hong Kong are known to be $39.5^{\circ}$ and $22.5^{\circ}$ respectively; on 6 June 2012 the transit times of Venus observed in Beijing and in Hong Kong were respectively $t_{\mathrm{P}}=6:21:57$ and $t_{\mathrm{P'}}=6:19:31$. Using these data and the conclusion of part iii), calculate the Sun–Earth distance $S_{\mathrm{SE}}$.

3) From the observations of the 1882 transit of Venus, the mean Sun–Earth distance was obtained as $S_{\mathrm{SE}}=1.5\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{km}$, and the diameter of the Sun as $D=1.4\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{km}$. The irradiance of solar radiation received by the Earth on a surface perpendicular to the direction of the solar radiation is $I=1.37\ \mathrm{kW\cdot m^{-2}}$. Find

i) the total energy received by the Earth from the Sun per unit time;

ii) the ratio of the energy consumed by the world population of 7 billion to the solar energy received by the Earth (assume that the annual energy consumption per person is 3 tonnes of standard coal, and that 1 kg of standard coal can generate 4 kWh of electricity);

iii) the total energy radiated by the Sun per unit time;

iv) estimate the surface temperature of the Sun.

4) i) Calculate the total mass and the mean density of the Sun;

ii) if the energy of the Sun came from chemical reactions, with the energy released per unit mass equal to that of coal, how long could it last, calculated with the energy the Sun now radiates per unit time? The Sun has existed as a star for about 5 billion years or more; by what factor, then, should its efficiency of energy production exceed that of chemical reactions?

5) Spectral analysis shows that the main constituent of the Sun is hydrogen; the basic nuclear fusion reactions involving hydrogen are as follows:

$$\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{P}\to\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{e}^{+}+\nu_{\mathrm{e}}\qquad\text{(a)}$$

$$\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{P}\to{}^{3}\mathrm{He}+\gamma\qquad\text{(b)}$$

$${}^{3}\mathrm{He}+{}^{3}\mathrm{He}\to{}^{4}\mathrm{He}+\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{P}\qquad\text{(c)}$$

The positrons produced in the above nuclear fusion processes will annihilate, and the neutrinos will escape. Atomic nuclei are all positively charged and repel one another; only when the temperature is very high can their kinetic energy overcome the Coulomb repulsion, so that fusion reactions take place. When the temperature is high enough, all atoms are ionized into atomic nuclei and electrons and are in a plasma state. (Here neglect the energy carried away by the neutrinos, and also the unfused hydrogen carried away by the solar wind.)

i) To maintain the radiation of the Sun, how many protons (hydrogen nuclei) must be consumed per unit time?

ii) At present 71% of the mass of the Sun is hydrogen; at this rate of consumption, for at most how many more years can it be maintained? Also calculate the proton–proton reaction probability per unit time (the ratio of the number of particles reacting per unit time to the total number of particles) $P_{\mathrm{PP}}$;

iii) the number of escaping neutrinos does not decrease during propagation; how many neutrinos reach the Earth per unit time per unit area perpendicular to the direction of the solar radiation? (The number of electron neutrinos actually reaching the Earth is only 35% of the theoretical value, but when the numbers of the other two kinds of neutrinos are added, it agrees with the theoretical value; this shows that some electron neutrinos are converted into other kinds of neutrinos during propagation, which is related to neutrino oscillations; the related achievements were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2002 and 2015.)

iv) How much mass does the Sun lose per unit time because of its radiation?

6) The probability $P$ of a fusion reaction depends on the temperature $T$ of the plasma, and the higher the particle number density $n$ (the number of particles per unit volume), the higher the reaction probability; the relation is $P=nR(T)$, where $R(T)$ is called the reaction rate. Fig. c gives the relation between the reaction rates of three kinds of fusion and the temperature; estimate the lower limit of the temperature of the solar core region (whose radius is about one quarter of the solar radius) in which nuclear fusion reactions can take place.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-1-6-fig3.png

Fig. c. Curves of the reaction rate versus temperature

7) Estimate the maximum energy carried away by a single neutrino, and estimate the maximum relative error of the calculation of the radiated energy in part 5) caused by neglecting the energy carried away by the neutrinos.

8) From the above calculations, the mass of the Sun decreases gradually; then the period and the mean orbital radius of the Earth's revolution around the Sun will also change. Calculate

i) the mass decrease $\Delta M$ due to radiation within one hundred million years;

ii) the resulting change of the period of the Earth's revolution.

As shown in Figure a, on a tour bus there is a three-legged round stool of radius $R$ (it may be regarded as a rigid structure). The lines joining the end points of the three identical stool legs (all horizontal) form an equilateral triangle of side $a$, and the centre of mass of the stool is at the point G on its axis. Problem 4

In September 2016 the G20 summit was held in Hangzhou. The decorative design of its conference hall showed both the energy-saving and environmental concepts of Chinese architecture and the characteristics of Zhejiang's bamboo culture. Figure a shows an enlarged photograph of part of the micro-perforated bamboo-panel decoration used on part of the walls; this decoration also achieves resonant absorption of sound waves. The bamboo panels have a series of rectangular micro-holes of different areas arranged periodically; after a sound wave enters a micro-hole, it makes the air column in the micro-hole perform simple harmonic vibrations. A single micro-hole together with the air layer behind the bamboo panel can be simplified as a Helmholtz resonator, as shown in Figure b. Assume that all micro-holes have depth $l$, that the volume of the air cavity behind a single micro-hole is $V_0$, and that the cross-sectional area of a micro-hole is $S$. The propagation of sound in the air layer may be regarded as an adiabatic process; the propagation speed $v_{\rm s}$ of sound is related to the air density $\rho$ and the bulk modulus $\kappa$ by

$$v_{\rm s} = \sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\rho}}$$

where $\kappa$ is the ratio of the increase $\Delta p$ in the gas pressure to the relative change of its volume $V$:

$$\kappa = -\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta V/V} = -V\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta V}$$

It is known that under standard conditions ($273\ {\rm K}$, $1\ {\rm atm} = 1.01\times10^{5}\ {\rm Pa}$) the molar mass of air (which may be regarded as an ideal gas) is $M_{\rm mol} = 29.0\ {\rm g/mol}$, the heat capacity ratio is $\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}$, and the universal gas constant is $R = 8.31\ {\rm J/(K\cdot mol)}$.

1) Find the density of air under standard conditions and the propagation speed $v_{\rm s}$ of sound in air;

2) Find the frequency of sound absorbed by the above Helmholtz resonator (expressed in terms of $v_{\rm s}$, $S$, $l$, $V_0$);

Problem 6

In cosmic rays there are large numbers of $\pi$ mesons flying at high speeds; they decay into a $\mu$ lepton and a $\mu$-type antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_\mu$:

$$\pi \to \mu + \bar{\nu}_\mu$$

The rest masses of the $\pi$ meson and of the $\mu$ lepton are known to be $m_\pi = 139.57061\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$ and $m_\mu = 105.65837\ {\rm MeV}/c^2$ respectively, and the rest mass of the antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_\mu$ is approximately zero. In the laboratory frame the speed of flight of the $\pi$ meson is measured to be $\boldsymbol{v} = 0.965\boldsymbol{c}$ ($c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ {\rm m/s}$ is the speed of light in vacuum).

1) Find the maximum and minimum speeds of the $\mu$ lepton produced in the above decay;

2) A $\mu$ lepton produced in the above decay flies vertically downward from a height of $10000\ {\rm m}$ above the ground. The half-life of the $\mu$ lepton at rest is known to be $T_{\frac{1}{2}}^{(0)} = 1.523\ \mu{\rm s}$. Find the maximum probability that an observer on the ground can observe the $\mu$ lepton.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

Lightning is one of the most spectacular natural phenomena on Earth. People have studied lightning extensively, and in recent years new phenomena have also been observed, such as transient luminous events and gamma-ray bursts caused by lightning. Lightning is usually produced by the discharge of thunderclouds (6–12 km above the ground); most lightning occurs inside the clouds and a small part reaches the ground. Because the ice-crystal particles inside the cloud collide with one another, the small ice-crystal particles become positively charged and float up with the air flow to the top of the cloud, while the larger particles become negatively charged and fall to the bottom of the cloud (see Figure a). Intra-cloud lightning neutralizes the positive and negative charges inside the cloud, whereas cloud-to-ground lightning releases the negative charge to the ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2019-2-7-fig1.png

Figure a. Schematic diagram of the charge distribution of a thundercloud

[Labels in the figure: 闪电 = lightning; 地面 = ground.]

1) The electric field inside a thundercloud in a certain cylindrical region high in the air is measured with an electric-field meter carried by a high-altitude balloon; its strength may be regarded as uniformly distributed, with magnitude $0.15\ {\rm MV/m}$. The central axis of this cylindrical region is perpendicular to the ground, its radius is $2.5\ {\rm km}$ and its height is $1.0\ {\rm km}$. Find the potential difference between the upper and lower ends of this region, the total amount of positive charge, and the total electric energy carried. The permittivity of vacuum is known to be $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ {\rm F/m}$.

2) During the electrification process, the charges at the upper and lower ends of a thundercloud increase exponentially with time. When the electric field at the Earth's surface exceeds $1.0\ {\rm kV/m}$, cloud-to-ground lightning occurs, so the surface electric field rarely exceeds $10\ {\rm kV/m}$. Suppose that the thundercloud described in 1) slowly moves downward as a whole from high in the air until its negative-charge layer is at a height of $6.0\ {\rm km}$ above the ground, where it temporarily remains stable. The ground is a good conductor. Estimate the strength of the surface electric field produced by this thundercloud directly below it.

3) Cloud-to-ground lightning is usually triggered by point discharge from the negatively charged ice-crystal particles at the bottom of a charged thundercloud: first a thin discharge path pointing toward the ground forms (with a diameter of the order of centimetres); this thin path extends downward with time and causes the surrounding air to be ionized continuously, gradually forming a thick cylindrical charged body with the original thin path as its axis (with cross-section of constant size), and finally a cloud-to-ground lightning channel forms near the ground. This lightning channel is perpendicular to the ground, the total amount of negative charge is $2.5\ {\rm C}$ (the charge in the original thin discharge path is relatively very small), and the electric field strength inside the lightning channel (excluding the central thin discharge path) is everywhere of the same magnitude. Assume that the length of the lightning channel is much greater than its diameter, that the diameter of the lightning channel is much greater than the diameter of the central thin discharge path, and that during the extremely short time before the lightning channel connects the cloud to the ground, the charge distribution inside the lightning channel may be regarded as steady. The breakdown threshold of the atmospheric electric field is known to be $3.0\ {\rm MV/m}$. Estimate the diameter of this cloud-to-ground lightning channel, and derive the expression for the radial distribution of the charge density inside the lightning channel (excluding the central thin discharge path).

4) After the lightning channel connects the cloud and the ground, the negative charges at the bottom of the cloud and inside the channel rapidly flow to the ground; the temperature of the lightning region suddenly rises to tens of thousands of degrees Celsius, so that the air in it is ionized and forms a plasma, emitting strong light, while the channel expands violently, producing thunder. The discharge current of the lightning can reach several tens of thousands of amperes within about $10\ \mu{\rm s}$. At the bottom of the channel (near the ground) strong radio waves with frequencies of about $30\ {\rm kHz}$ are radiated in all directions. Since electromagnetic waves with frequencies below $20\ {\rm MHz}$ (the so-called ionospheric cut-off frequency) cannot enter the interior of the ionosphere, these radio waves heat the plasma at the bottom of the ionosphere (about $80\ {\rm km}$ above the ground); once the lightning current exceeds a certain threshold, this causes the bottom of the ionosphere to glow instantaneously, forming a ring of light centred at the bottom of the ionosphere directly above the source of the strong radio waves (the bottom of the channel), whose maximum diameter can extend to several hundred kilometres. Sketch a diagram of the physical process of the formation and expansion of the ring of light at the bottom of the ionosphere, and calculate the radial speed of expansion of the ring of light when its radius is $100\ {\rm km}$.

5) The microwave-bubble model of ball lightning holds that ball lightning is a spherical plasma microwave cavity (bubble). When the lightning microwaves are rather weak and insufficient to form a microwave bubble, they radiate toward outer space and pass through the ionosphere, and can be observed by satellites. In fact, satellites have indeed observed this kind of microwave radiation. However, the signals observed by satellites are easily disturbed by ionospheric dispersion, whereas a high-altitude balloon carrying a detector can reach above the thundercloud for observation, so as to avoid such disturbances. In order to observe, at a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground, the microwave signals emitted by lightning, a high-altitude helium balloon with a payload (including the balloon material and the detector) of $50\ {\rm kg}$ is to be kept floating in this region. Find the volume of this balloon when it floats in that high-altitude region. It is known that below a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground the atmospheric temperature decreases by $5.0\ {\rm K}$ for every $1\ {\rm km}$ rise in height; the ground temperature is $T_0 = 290\ {\rm K}$, the ground pressure is $p_0 = 1.01\times10^{5}\ {\rm pa}$, the molar mass of air is $M = 29\ {\rm g/mol}$; the density of helium in the balloon (its value at a height of $12\ {\rm km}$ above the ground) is $\rho_{\rm He} = 0.18\ {\rm kg/m^3}$; the gravitational acceleration is $g = 9.8\ {\rm m/s^2}$, and the universal gas constant is $R = 8.31\ {\rm J/(K\cdot mol)}$.

problems.title: Problem 1

Problem 1

China's large scientific facility, the Spallation Neutron Source, was completed and put into operation in 2018; it has wide applications in many fields. Historically, Chadwick first confirmed the existence of the neutron in 1932 and measured its mass; in 1939 Hahn and co-workers discovered that bombarding uranium nuclei with neutrons can make them split, at the same time releasing neutrons and triggering a chain reaction. In order for the chain reaction to proceed in a sustained and controllable way, the neutrons released by the uranium nuclei can be slowed down (moderated) by elastic collisions. Relativistic effects are not to be considered.

(1) Chadwick bombarded stationary target nuclei of mass $m_1$ (hydrogen nuclei H or nitrogen nuclei $^{14}\mathrm{N}$, of mass $m_{\mathrm{H}}$ or $14m_{\mathrm{H}}$) with neutrons (of mass $m$) and observed their motion. Let the angle between the outgoing momentum of the target nucleus and the initial momentum of the incident neutron be $\alpha$. Derive the relations of the outgoing speed $v_1$ of the target nucleus and of the final speed $v$ of the neutron, respectively, to the initial speed $v_0$ of the neutron. In this experiment the maximum outgoing speed of the hydrogen nuclei was measured to be $3.30\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the maximum outgoing speed of the nitrogen nuclei $4.70\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the values of $m$ and $v_0$.

(2) In the above experiment a nitrogen nucleus may also be struck successively by a beam of neutrons. Suppose the nitrogen nucleus is initially at rest, every neutron colliding with it has speed $v_0$, and every collision gives the largest possible increase of the speed of the nitrogen nucleus. Calculate after how many collisions the kinetic energy of the nitrogen nucleus is approximately equal to the initial kinetic energy of a neutron.

(3) Suppose the neutrons slowed down by many collisions are in thermal equilibrium, their speeds obeying the Maxwell distribution

$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)^{3/2}v^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{mv^{2}}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}},$$

where $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the system. Calculate, at thermal equilibrium, the kinetic energy corresponding to the most probable speed of the neutrons, and the most probable kinetic energy.

problems.title: Problem 2

Problem 2

When two conducting spheres in an electric field come close to each other, the electric field between the conducting spheres is markedly enhanced. This problem explores this phenomenon. The vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ is known.

(1) The centre of an isolated conducting sphere of radius $R_0$ is at distance $a$ ($a>R_0$) from a stationary point charge $Q$. Find the magnitude of the image charge and its position.

(2) The conducting sphere is placed in a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$; this external field can be regarded as produced, at the midpoint of the line joining them, by two equal and opposite point charges $\pm Q$ very far apart. Prove that the action of the induced charge of the conducting sphere is equivalent to an electric dipole formed by two image charges, and find the relation between the dipole moment of this electric dipole and the external field $E_0$.

(3) Outside the conducting sphere, two equal and opposite point charges $\pm q$ are separated by $\Delta l$; the electric dipole $q\Delta\boldsymbol{l}$ they form is placed radially near the conducting sphere of radius $R_0$, with the centre of the dipole at distance $r$ ($r\gg\Delta l$) from the centre of the conducting sphere. Find the magnitude of the image dipole moment of this dipole in the conducting sphere.

(4) In a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$, two conducting spheres of radius $R_0$ are placed along the direction of the external field, their centres a distance $r$ ($r>2R_0$) apart. Find the distribution of the electric potential at any point $\mathrm{P}'(x,y)$ outside the conducting spheres in the plane through the two centres, and the distribution of the field strength along the direction of the line joining the two centres (recurrence relations may be used). Take the midpoint of the line joining the two centres as the origin of coordinates and the direction of this line as the $X$ axis.

(5) Prove that, if breakdown discharge is not considered, when the above two conductors are slowly brought infinitely close to each other, the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining the centres of the two spheres tends to infinity because of electrostatic induction.

problems.title: Problem 3

Problem 3

A quantum heat engine is a heat engine that runs a cycle with quantum matter as the working substance. Below, a two-level atomic system is taken as an example to describe the working principle of a quantum heat engine. The average energy of a two-level atom is defined as

$$\langle E\rangle=p_0\cdot E_0+p_1\cdot E_1,$$

where $E_0$, $p_0$ and $E_1$, $p_1$ denote the energies and probabilities of the atom being in the ground state and in the excited state, respectively. For simplicity, assume $E_0=0$; during the cycle the energy difference between the excited state and the ground state is an adjustable parameter. The probability that the atom is in a state of energy $E$ obeys the Boltzmann distribution

$$p\propto\mathrm{e}^{-E/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)},$$

where $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature and $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant. In a quasi-static process the change of the average energy is

$$\mathrm{d}\langle E\rangle=p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1+E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1,$$

where $p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the energy level, corresponding to the work $\text{đ}W$ done by the surroundings on the two-level atomic system, and $E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the probability, corresponding to the heat $\text{đ}Q$ transferred by the surroundings to the two-level atomic system.

(1) The two-level atomic system is put in contact with a heat reservoir of temperature $T$. Find the probability $p_0$ that the two-level atomic system is in the ground state and the probability $p_1$ that it is in the excited state at thermal equilibrium.

(2) The $P$-$V$ diagram of the classical Otto cycle is shown in Figure 2a, where A→B and C→D are isochoric processes and B→C and D→A are adiabatic processes. Sketch the relation between the energy difference $E_1$ of the two levels and the excited-state probability $p_1$ during the quantum Otto cycle, and calculate the heat transferred, the increase of internal energy and the work done on the surroundings in each of the four processes of the quantum Otto cycle.

Figure 2a [绝热 = adiabatic]

Assuming that the temperature $T_h$ of the hot reservoir and the temperature $T_l$ of the cold reservoir in the quantum Carnot cycle are equal, respectively, to the highest and the lowest temperature of the quantum Otto cycle, compare the efficiencies of the quantum Otto engine and the quantum Carnot engine.

Problem 5

Interstellar medium exists in the vast cosmic space between the stars. Under the action of cosmic rays, molecules of the interstellar medium lose some of their electrons and become positive ions, while the electrons wander free, forming a plasma state. A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star with an extremely strong magnetic field; the electromagnetic radiation from it observed on the Earth is a pulsed signal. Pulsar signals can be used for interstellar navigation and high-precision timekeeping; for this it is necessary to obtain the precise times of arrival of the pulses at the Earth, and to study the phase changes and dispersion of their electromagnetic radiation.

The distance from a pulsar to the Earth is $d$, and the mean number density of electrons in the interstellar medium is $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ (of the order of $10^{4}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$). Assume that there is a uniform static magnetic field $B$ in the medium (of the order of $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{T}$), directed parallel to the propagation direction of the electromagnetic waves. The electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the electron charge $-e$ ($e>0$), the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ and the speed of light in vacuum $c$ are known.

(1) Take the direction of the electromagnetic radiation from the pulsar to the Earth as the positive $z$ direction. For an electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ the electric field is $E_x=E_0\cos(kz-2\pi ft)$, $E_y=E_0\cos\left(kz-2\pi ft\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $E_0$ and $k$ are the amplitude and the wave number of the electromagnetic wave, respectively. For simplicity, take $E_0$ to be constant and neglect the action of the magnetic field of the electromagnetic wave itself on the electrons. Find the gyration radius $R_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the electron motion.

(2) When a pulsar signal propagates in the interstellar medium, dispersion occurs; its propagation speed (the magnitude $v_{\mathrm{g}}$ of the group velocity) depends on the rate of change of the frequency of the electromagnetic wave with respect to the wave number: $v_{\mathrm{g}}=2\pi\dfrac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}k}$. Find the lowest frequency $f_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the electromagnetic waves of the pulsar signal that can pass through the medium and reach the Earth.

(3) Assuming that the mean electron number density $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the interstellar medium stays constant along the propagation path of the pulsar signal, by how much is the time of arrival at the Earth of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal delayed compared with its propagation time in vacuum?

(4) It is observed that the electromagnetic waves of frequency $f$ that leave the pulsar simultaneously show a phase difference on arrival at the Earth. Find this phase difference (the approximations $\dfrac{e}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{e}}}{\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm{e}}}}\ll f$, $\dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_{\mathrm{e}}}\ll f$ may be used).

(5) If over an interval of length $a$ along the propagation path the electron number density shows a fluctuation $\Delta n_{\mathrm{e}}$, find the phase shift, caused by the fluctuation of the electron number density, of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal after it passes through this interval.

Antiprotons can be produced by bombarding a stationary proton target with a beam of high-energy protons of energy $6.8\,\mathrm{GeV}$ per particle; the reaction is

$$\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}\to\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}+\underbrace{\mathrm{p}+\bar{\mathrm{p}}}_{\hookrightarrow\ \pi^{-}+\cdots}$$

When protons and antiprotons annihilate, $\pi^{-}$ mesons can be produced, so the antiproton beam is also accompanied by a large number of $\pi^{-}$ mesons. A Cherenkov counter determines the speed of a charged particle by detecting Cherenkov radiation (the electromagnetic radiation excited when a charged particle moves in a medium faster than the speed of light in the medium). $\mathrm{C}_1$ records only the faster $\pi^{-}$ mesons, and $\mathrm{C}_2$ records only the slower antiprotons. If a $\pi^{-}$ meson has the same kinetic energy as the antiproton, find the time $t_{\pi^{-}}$ the $\pi^{-}$ meson needs to travel from $\mathrm{S}_1$ to $\mathrm{S}_2$.

(2) A charged particle moving with speed $v$ ($v>c/n$) passes through a medium of refractive index $n$. Find the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation produced and the direction of motion of the charged particle.

When the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation and the direction of motion of the charged particle is very small, the spherical mirror focuses the Cherenkov radiation excited by the charged particle onto its focal plane, forming a ring of radiation of radius $r$, which is projected onto the counters. Problem 7

According to the chapter "Youzuo" of the Xunzi (《荀子·宥坐篇》), Confucius visited the ancestral temple of Duke Huan of Lu, where there was a qi (欹, qī) vessel, a "tilting vessel". Of the tilting vessel it is said: "When empty it tilts, when moderately filled it stands upright, when full it overturns." A real suspended tilting vessel is shown in Figure 7a: when the vessel is empty, its body is tilted; when moderately filled with water, its body stands upright; when filled with too much water, its body overturns. Figure 7b is the front cross-sectional view of the suspended tilting vessel. The outer contour of the whole vessel is a surface of revolution about the $Z$ axis; the $Z'$ axis is the symmetry axis of the bored inner cavity. The radii of the hemispherical shells of the inner wall and of the outer wall of the vessel are $R_1=R$ and $R_2=\sqrt{3}R$, respectively, and the centres $O$ and $O'$ of the two hemispheres both lie on the $X$ axis. The straight line through the pair of suspension points of the vessel intersects the $XOZ$ plane at the point $Q$, whose coordinates are $(x_Q=-R/10,\ z_Q=2\sqrt{3}R/11)$. Problem 1

[40 points] The smooth running of a high-speed train is closely related to the degree of vibration of the train; air springs installed on the train can effectively damp vibrations. The air-spring model used in a certain high-speed-train test experiment consists of a main air chamber (an air bag) and an auxiliary air chamber (of constant volume), as shown in Figure 1a. The vertically upward force exerted by the air spring on the sprung load is provided by the elastic force produced by the compressed air inside the air bag. When the sprung load is in equilibrium, the pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber are $p_{10}$ and $V_{10}$ respectively, the volume of the auxiliary air chamber is $V_2$, and the atmospheric pressure is $p_0$. The ratio of the vertically upward force $F$ of the air spring to the difference between the pressure of the gas in the main air chamber and the atmospheric pressure is called the effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the air spring. The molar heat capacity of air at constant volume is known to be $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ ($R$ is the universal gas constant). Assume that, under small-amplitude vibration, both the volume $V_1$ of the gas in the main air chamber and the effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$ can be regarded as linear functions of the vertical displacement $y$ (positive downward) of the bearing surface of the air spring (air bag) relative to its equilibrium position, with rates of change equal to the constants $-\alpha$ ($\alpha > 0$) and $\beta$ ($\beta > 0$) respectively.

Figure 1a

(1) With the auxiliary air chamber not connected to the main air chamber (valve closed), derive, in each of the following two cases, the relation between the stiffness $K \equiv \mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}y$ of the air spring and its effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$:

i) passengers getting on and off (the changes of pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber follow an isothermal process);

ii) the train meets violent jolting while running (the changes of pressure and volume of the gas in the main air chamber follow an adiabatic process).

(2) With the main air chamber connected to the auxiliary air chamber (valve open), derive, in the two cases above, the relation between the stiffness $K$ of the air spring and its effective bearing area $A_{\mathrm{e}}$. Problem 2

[40 points] A homogeneous solid cue ball of mass $m$ and radius $R$ rests on a horizontal table; the coefficient of sliding friction between the cue ball and the table is $\mu$. The cue is adjusted so that it lies horizontally in the vertical plane through the centre of the ball, and it strikes the upper half of the cue ball; the height of the cue relative to the horizontal plane containing the centre of the ball is $R/2$, and the duration of the strike is extremely short. The impulse received by the cue ball has magnitude $P$ and is horizontal. Assume that the maximum static friction force equals the sliding friction force. The magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

(1) How long after the strike does the cue ball begin pure rolling? Find the velocity of the centre of the ball when the cue ball reaches pure rolling.

(2) Let B be the point of the cue ball in contact with the table at the moment when the cue ball reaches pure rolling (take this moment as the zero of time). Find the position, velocity and acceleration of the point B on the ball at a subsequent time $t'$.

Problem 3

[40 points] The negative differential resistance effect is the property of certain circuits or electronic components (such as the tunnel diode) that, within a particular voltage range, their current decreases as the terminal voltage increases; this effect can sustain high-frequency oscillations in a circuit and output an amplified AC signal. In the simplified circuit shown in Figure 3a, D is a tunnel diode. On its left side there is a fixed resistor $R$, an inductor $L$ and a capacitor $C$ connected in series; the AC current in this loop is denoted by $i(t)$. On its right side there is an ideal high-frequency choke RFC (zero DC resistance, completely blocking AC signals) and an ideal constant-voltage DC source $V_0$; the DC current in this loop is denoted by $I$ ($I \gg |i(t)|$). The positive directions of the currents are marked in the figure. D always stays within the particular voltage range, in which its resistance is $-R_0$ ($R_0 > 0$, and is a constant).

(1) It is known that at $t = 0$, $i(0) = 0$ and $\dot{i}(0) = \beta \neq 0$ ($\dot{a}$ denotes the derivative of $a$ with respect to $t$); the AC current varies with time according to

$$i(t) = \alpha_1 e^{\beta_1 t} + \alpha_2 e^{\beta_2 t}, \quad (\alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \beta_2 \text{ are constants to be determined})$$

Determine the constants $\alpha_1$, $\beta_1$, $\alpha_2$, $\beta_2$, so as to determine the AC current $i(t)$ at any time $t$.

(2) Explain under what condition resonance (harmonic oscillation) occurs in the left loop. Find the current $i_{\mathrm{H}}(t)$ in the left loop and the resonance frequency $f_{\mathrm{H}}$ in the case of resonance.

Find the maximum average power $\bar{P}_{\max}$ that the AC part on the tunnel diode can reach, and the output voltage $V_0$ of the ideal constant-voltage DC source in that case.

Problem 4

[40 points] In 1930 Lawrence (E. O. Lawrence) first proposed the principle of the cyclotron: two semicircular magnetic fields make charged particles revolve along arc-shaped orbits, and the particles obtain high energies by being accelerated repeatedly by the high-frequency electric field in the gap between the two semicircles. For this highly creative scheme he received the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics.

(1) At present the largest circular accelerator in the world is the high-energy proton synchrotron Tevatron at Fermilab (the circumference of the largest circular orbit of the particles is $L_{\max} = 6436\,\mathrm{m}$), which can accelerate a proton to a maximum energy of $E_{\mathrm{p},\max}^{(\mathrm{tevatron})} = 1.00\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Assume that during acceleration the proton always moves in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, and neglect energy losses due to electromagnetic radiation. Find the minimum value $B_{\min}$ of the magnetic induction needed by the synchrotron Tevatron to accelerate protons to the above maximum energy.

(2) A high-energy incident proton bombarding a stationary proton (the target proton) can produce an antiproton $\bar{\mathrm{p}}$, according to the reaction

$$\mathrm{p} + \mathrm{p} \rightarrow \mathrm{p} + \mathrm{p} + \mathrm{p} + \bar{\mathrm{p}}$$

Find the minimum kinetic energy of the incident proton for which antiprotons can be produced, and determine whether the protons accelerated by the Tevatron of part (1) can produce antiprotons by bombarding stationary target protons.

Given data: proton mass $m_{\mathrm{p}} = 938.3\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^2$, speed of light in vacuum $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Problem 6

[40 points] The fibre-optic gyroscope is an optical instrument that can determine precisely the orientation of a moving object; it is an inertial navigation instrument widely used in modern fields such as navigation at sea, aviation and spaceflight. Fibre-optic gyroscope navigation is based mainly on the following effect: in a fibre-optic loop of radius $R$ rotating with angular velocity $\Omega$ (see Figure 6a), two coherent beams split off by the beam splitter A fixed on the loop propagate counterclockwise (CCW) and clockwise (CW) respectively and then return to A, and their optical path lengths are different. By detecting the phase difference of the two beams or the change of the interference fringes, the rotational angular velocity $\Omega$ of the fibre loop can be determined. The speed of light in vacuum is $c$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-2-6-fig1.png

Figure 6a

(1) As shown in Figure 6b, the optical fibre consists of an inner and an outer layer of media, with refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$ respectively ($n_1 > n_2$). In order for light to be transmitted inside the fibre, what condition must the angle of incidence $i$ of the light at the input port (the refractive index of the medium outside the port is $n_0$) satisfy?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-2-6-fig2.png

Figure 6b

(2) Consider $N$ turns of optical fibre wound closely along the loop, joined end to end at the beam splitter A; the fibre loop rotates counterclockwise with angular velocity $\Omega$. Two coherent beams split off from A propagate counterclockwise and clockwise along the fibre loop and return to A. The refractive index of the medium in which the light propagates is known to be $n_1$, and the wavelength of the two beams in vacuum is $\lambda_0$. What are the times $t_{\mathrm{CCW}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{CW}}$ taken by the two coherent beams to propagate counterclockwise and clockwise respectively along the fibre loop? What is the phase difference of the two beams? Point out the relation between this phase difference and the refractive index $n_1$ of the medium.

(3) In order to increase the degree of miniaturization of gyroscope systems, a resonant optical gyroscope system has been proposed. This system contains an optical ring cavity rotating counterclockwise, of radius $R$ and rotational angular velocity $\Omega$ ($R\Omega \ll c$); the refractive index of the medium in the cavity is known to be $n$. In the cavity there exist two classes of resonant modes, propagating counterclockwise and clockwise. When the ring cavity is at rest, the wavelengths $\lambda_{m0}$ of these modes are determined by the periodic boundary condition $2\pi R = m\lambda_{m0}$, where $m$ is a positive integer, called the order of the resonant mode. When the ring cavity rotates, there is a resonance-frequency difference $\Delta f$ between the clockwise- and counterclockwise-propagating resonant modes of the same order (both $m$). Derive the relation between the rotational angular velocity $\Omega$ of the ring cavity and this resonance-frequency difference $\Delta f$.

Problem 7

[40 points] In 2015 the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) detected for the first time the gravitational waves produced by the merger of a binary black hole a billion light years away, confirming the predictions of Einstein's theory of the existence of gravitational waves and black holes. The black-hole merger process is divided into three stages. In the first stage (the inspiral stage), the two black holes move in approximately circular orbits about the centre of mass of the system in the same plane (see Figure 7a); the mechanical energy lost is converted into gravitational radiation energy, and the two gradually approach each other along spirals. In the second stage (the merger stage), the binary black hole merges into one black hole. In the last stage (the ringdown stage), the merged black hole relaxes to an equilibrium state and becomes a stable rotating black hole. In the inspiral stage, if the spins and sizes of the black holes are neglected, the two black holes can be regarded as point masses of constant masses $M$ and $m$ respectively, and the distance $L$ between them gradually decreases with time. Assume that the system has no energy dissipation other than the radiation of gravitational waves, do not consider the back-reaction of the gravitational radiation, and use Newtonian gravitational theory as an approximation.

Choose three physical quantities that describe the radiation of a rotating system and, together with $G$, derive the expression for the radiated power of gravitational waves (assume that the dimensionless proportionality constant that may remain undetermined in it is $\alpha$).

(2) If at the initial moment $t = 0$ the distance between the two black holes is $L_0$, and the dimensionless proportionality constant $\alpha$ in the expression for the radiated power of gravitational waves is known, find the time needed for the two black holes to revolve through $360^\circ$ about the centre of mass of the system starting from $t = 0$.

Problem 8

[40 points] The process of modulating an electrically transmitted signal onto an optical signal is called electro-optic modulation. The main working principle of an electro-optic modulator is the electro-optic effect: taking a lithium niobate electro-optic crystal as an example, its refractive index changes under the action of an electric field, thereby changing the optical path of the input light beam, so that the information of the electrical signal is transferred to the optical signal. The optical path of the electro-optic modulator is shown in Figure 8a. $\mathrm{P_1}$ and $\mathrm{P_2}$ are the polarizer and the analyzer respectively; the two have the same structure but mutually perpendicular polarization directions (in the figure, $\mathrm{P_1}(\parallel x_1)$ and $\mathrm{P_2}(\parallel x_2)$ indicate that the polarization directions of $\mathrm{P_1}$ and $\mathrm{P_2}$ are parallel to the $x_1$ and $x_2$ coordinate axes respectively). An electro-optic crystal of length $l$ and thickness $d$ is placed between $\mathrm{P_1}$ and $\mathrm{P_2}$, and a voltage $V$ is applied between the two end faces of the crystal (so as to produce an electric field along the $x_3$ direction, of magnitude $E$). A light wave of vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$, after passing through the polarizer $\mathrm{P_1}$ ($\parallel x_1$), is incident on the electro-optic crystal along the $x_3$ direction and, after refraction, splits into two light waves with mutually perpendicular polarization directions (parallel to the fast axis $x_1'$ and the slow axis $x_2'$ respectively); the $x_1'$ axis makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the $x_1$ axis, and so does the $x_2'$ axis with the $x_2$ axis. The refractive indices in the electro-optic crystal along the $x_1'$ and $x_2'$ directions are respectively

$$\begin{cases} n_{x_1'} = n_{\mathrm{o}} - \dfrac{1}{2}n_{\mathrm{o}}^{3}\gamma E \\[2mm] n_{x_2'} = n_{\mathrm{o}} + \dfrac{1}{2}n_{\mathrm{o}}^{3}\gamma E \end{cases}$$

where $n_{\mathrm{o}}$ is the refractive index for the o-ray and $\gamma$ is a constant determined by the properties of the crystal itself. After leaving the electro-optic crystal, the two light beams pass through a 1/4-wave plate and are finally collected by the analyzer $\mathrm{P_2}$ ($\parallel x_2$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-2-8-fig1.png

Figure 8a

[Labels in the figure: 入射光束 = incident light beam; 外加电压 = applied voltage; 1/4波片 = quarter-wave plate; 出射光束 = emergent light beam.]

(1) A light beam of angular frequency $\omega$ is incident on the left end face of the electro-optic crystal, with electric field

$$\begin{cases} E_{x_1'} = E_0\cos\omega t \\ E_{x_2'} = E_0\cos\omega t \end{cases}$$

Find the phase change and the intensity change of the light after it passes through the electro-optic crystal. When the phase difference between the emergent light beams is $\pi$, the electro-optic crystal acts as a "half-wave plate"; the applied voltage used in this case is called the half-wave voltage $V_\pi$. Find $V_\pi$.

(2) Let the applied electrical signal voltage be

$$V = V_{\mathrm{m}}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{m}} t \qquad (V_{\mathrm{m}} \ll V_\pi)$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ is the frequency of the modulating signal. If the light wave enters the analyzer $\mathrm{P_2}$ directly without passing through the 1/4-wave plate, find the relation between the intensity transmittance of the emergent beam (the ratio of the emergent to the incident light intensity) and the electrical signal voltage. Only when the transmittance of the electro-optic modulator has a good linear relation with the modulating voltage is the signal undistorted after the electrical signal has been transferred to the optical signal. Find the relation between the intensity transmittance of the emergent beam and the electrical signal voltage when the light passes through the 1/4-wave plate and the analyzer $\mathrm{P_2}$, and point out the role played by the 1/4-wave plate.

(3) The equivalent circuit of the electro-optic modulator is shown in the left half of Figure 8b: the electro-optic crystal is placed between two parallel-plate electrodes, and the electro-optic crystal between the two parallel plates can be treated as equivalent to a resistance-capacitance parallel circuit consisting of a resistance $R$ and a capacitance $C$; $V$ is the applied signal voltage, and $R_{\mathrm{m}}$ is the resistance of the modulating source and the wires; usually $R \gg R_{\mathrm{m}}$. Prove that, with the switches in Figure 8b open, when $\omega_{\mathrm{m}} \gg (R_{\mathrm{m}}C)^{-1}$ the voltage $V_{\mathrm{c}}$ actually applied to the electro-optic crystal satisfies $|V_{\mathrm{c}}| \ll |V|$, i.e. the modulation efficiency is extremely low.

Figure 8b

[Labels in the figure: 外加电压 = applied voltage; 电光晶体 = electro-optic crystal.]

Prove that $|V_{\mathrm{c}}| \approx |V|$.
